description: I Am The Cavalry talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: I am the Cavalry
talks.teaser: Covers how cyber disruption to water and hospitals could strain communities, and how local volunteers can prepare.
talks.summary:
The session opens with an emergency manager, Sarah Miller, arguing that preparedness is measured by the actions people take rather than the kits they own. She addresses common myths about panic and looting after disasters, explains why federal help may arrive more slowly, and argues that messages work better when they are tailored, repeated and delivered by trusted local peers. Her examples include neighborhood mapping programs, basic first aid training and getting to know neighbors before a crisis.

Mark Montgomery, a retired rear admiral, then describes what he sees as a serious national security risk. He points to Chinese pre-positioning inside US infrastructure, often called Volt Typhoon, and to military mobility depending on civilian rail, ports and airports run by thinly resourced local operators. He argues that water systems are especially exposed and that a disruption would quickly affect hospitals, and he links the timing of that risk to the Taiwan situation.

Josh Corman then presents the Undisruptible 27 project, which works with hospital communities to convene water, healthcare, city planning, power and emergency management stakeholders. Pilot work favors simple engineering controls, such as pressure sensors and surge relief, at a cost of roughly ten thousand dollars per town. He closes with homework for attendees: raising questions at local meetings, drafting household continuity guidance, contacting elected officials and joining working groups.

talks.title: I am the Cavalry
talks.teaser: Covers critical infrastructure resilience, from low-cost emergency radio alerts to grid supply chains and end-of-life device policy.
talks.summary:
The recording opens with a LoRa-based emergency broadcast project built on cheap radios. The presenters argue that sirens and SaaS notification tools are expensive or unreliable when power, phones and internet fail, and they propose a one-way, digitally signed alert channel. They demonstrate low-cost receiver nodes that blink or buzz on high-priority messages and cover build costs and range limits.

Later sessions move to critical infrastructure. One speaker traces intrusions into internet-exposed water utility controllers and explains how adversaries use rotating proxy networks, which makes indicator blocking ineffective and makes takedowns temporary. Another covers data center load growth on the electric grid, oscillation events, and the share of grid hardware sourced from adversarial countries. A further session describes a 100-day effort to help under-resourced operational technology operators reduce risk, and CISA outlines CI Fortify, which asks operators to isolate their systems and test recovery without phones or internet.

The day closes with a discussion of abandoned devices. Speakers argue that vendors should disclose support windows, keep end-of-life products safe, and reconsider the costs they push onto customers, and another talk urges designing infrastructure to be disposable and distributed rather than irreplaceable. The practical takeaways are to plan for degraded communications, rehearse recovery, and treat vendor support lifecycles as a security risk.

talks.title: I am the Cavalry
talks.teaser: Sets the stakes for a track on protecting water, hospitals and other lifelines from state-backed disruption.
talks.summary:
Josh Corman opens the I am the Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas, marking the initiative's thirteenth year. He frames the core problem as society's growing reliance on connected software in public-safety systems such as water, power, medical devices and hospitals, and argues that this dependence has outpaced our ability to secure it. He describes how the group's Undisruptible 27 effort has shifted toward target-rich but cyber-poor operators, aiming to fund practical engineering mitigations for water utilities that serve hospitals.

He then walks through the threat picture. He cites recent activity against programmable logic controllers in water utilities, the Volt Typhoon prepositioning in US infrastructure, and a possible Taiwan contingency timeline. He argues that availability matters more than confidentiality in operational technology, and that denial of service can cause real harm without any remote code execution. He also critiques the assumption that AI-driven vulnerability discovery is addressed by patch creation alone, since many operators cannot patch quickly or at all.

The talk closes by previewing the rest of the track, which covers engineering-based defenses, hospital continuity, communications, food supply and emergency management. The speaker asks attendees to engage with their local municipal leaders and to bring concrete, actionable ideas back to their communities rather than treating the problem as a spectator sport.
